summary:
Andalucía stands under Spain's national framework: Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the organic law on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGTBI rights, applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, Andalucía included. The regional position on legal gender recognition is therefore set by national statute rather than by any Andalucía-specific instrument.

Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis or prior medical treatment; the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Spanish Constitution. Recognition is available from age 12 under conditions, and the statute regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

The same statute bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expands assisted-reproduction rules, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and adds anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. It defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges collection of discrimination data broken down by the covered causes, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances.

Gender expression appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance of Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023, so a crime motivated by gender identity or expression is charged through general offences with the discrimination aggravation instead of a free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 separately reformed offences against sexual freedom in Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

That machinery is being applied in practice. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In January 2026 the Observatorio de delitos de odio reported a Valencia case in which a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them: the sole adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Protection is not uniform across Spain. In 2023 the newly elected regional government of Madrid repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed penalties for conversion therapy and repealed several trans legal recognitions.

Facility access rests on legal gender self-determination under the current framework, according to reporting of 9 July 2026, which contrasts Spain with the United Kingdom's move toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code, where restrictions apply case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005, and legal gender change requires no surgery or sterilisation. Official and industry framing is favourable: UK foreign travel advice describes Spain as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities and social venues, and a travel operator guide rates the country safe and welcoming, especially Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting that attitudes outside the large cities can be more conservative.

Protection against anti-trans hostility is not uniform across Spain's autonomous communities. In 2023 the newly elected regional government of Madrid repealed that region's non-discrimination law, repealed the local conversion therapy ban insofar as it applies to trans people, removed penalties for conversion therapy and repealed several trans legal recognitions. Andalucía has not been reported as following that course, but the divergence shows that the national floor does not describe every region's practice.

Official and industry framing of Spain as a destination is favourable. UK foreign travel advice describes Spain as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers with active communities and social venues, and a travel operator guide rates the country safe and welcoming, especially Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting that attitudes outside the large cities can be more conservative. Andalucía's own cities, including Seville and Málaga, sit within that same pattern of more permissive urban centres and more conservative rural areas, and the national statute mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Andalucía-specific instrument on trans legal recognition, conversion therapy, facility access or regional enforcement was identified in the source inventory; the region's position is carried by the national statute. Whether Andalucía's regional government has adopted or repealed any complementary measures beyond Ley 4/2023 is unresolved and not sourced here.

The two enforcement incidents cited, in Vigo and Valencia, are drawn from other autonomous communities and illustrate the national machinery in practice rather than Andalucía's own docket.
